correctness.rationale: The graph, leader budget, normalization and empty-part boundary cases are explicit. The positive grounded matrix has trace (1) obtained via a rank-one block inverse. Exact rational identity (3) makes every mixed allocation for k<=m strictly worse than a pure endpoint, and identity (2) compares the endpoints by sign of k^2-(2m+1), including every tie. For k>=m+1, identity (4) is strictly positive when any vertex of the larger part remains a follower. These statements prove all infinite parameter cases and counts, not merely finite enumeration. The exact-rational standard-library verification replayed 353496 allocation cases, 166650 strict-chord cases, 220 independently assembled grounded inverses and 666 labeled subset inverses.

originality.rationale: Known generic leader-selection and joint-centrality formulas do not supply the sharp all-budget threshold, the strict pure-part classification for K_{m,m+1}, or all optimizer counts. The closest earlier fixed-budget result is the complete-bipartite classification for exactly three leaders, which contains the K_{4,5} three-leader tie but cannot imply the classification for arbitrary budgets. A relevant published mathematical record concerns discounted hitting domination, a distinct objective. Actual semantic mathematical-record and targeted source searches did not identify an equivalent or stronger statement; this absence is not a uniqueness certificate and specialized literature remains a residual risk.
residual_risks: A specialized or incompletely indexed exact leader-selection paper could state the same square-root switching theorem or a dominating arbitrary-budget biclique result.

value.rationale: A practically motivated fixed-budget H2 leader-placement problem on the canonical minimally imbalanced biclique family is solved for every budget, with all minimizers and counts. The exact square-root threshold k^2=2m+1 forces discontinuous relocation of the entire optimal leader set and forbids any nested optimal budget sequence, a precise obstruction to sequential expansion in an elementary network class. The key strict chord inequality excludes all mixed candidates. This is stronger than routine endpoint evaluation or a fixed-three-leader exercise: the arbitrary-budget transition and optimizer census have independent precise use when planning the leader budget.
